newsitem.title: PERU: Peru stoic as hostage crisis overshadows Christmas.
newsitem.headline: Peru stoic as hostage crisis overshadows Christmas.

text.p: Wishes for "peace and joy" rang hollow in Lima on Wednesday as Peruvians celebrated Christmas Day and prayed for Marxist rebels to free their 105 hostages.

The rich attended a formal, black-tie concert and mass in Lima's cathedral beneath an opulent banner spelling out "peace", while the Salvation Army handed out plastic cups of hot chocolate at a vigil outside the besieged Japanese ambassador's residence in the San Isidro district.

"Dad, we love you. We want you to have a happy Christmas and continue being the great father that you are," Napoleon Rivas said outside the residence, echoing the emotional messages aired on national radio by scores of relatives, hopeful the hostages were listening from within the fortified compound.

Choir harmonies from a few blocks away drifted toward the luxury residence. A dozen teenagers carried bibles to be taken into the embassy compound where a captive Jesuit priest held a mass lit by candles supplied by the Red Cross.
"We've put messages in the bibles telling the hostages we are praying with them for their release," said Oswaldo Melgarejo.

"We are adding our little grain of sand," said Violeta Giraldo, a Salvation Army volunteer handing out a traditional hot chocolate drink to hostages' relatives, who flocked to the site to be nearer their loved ones.
"Inside they must be able to sense all the good feeling here, all the positive energy as everybody wants them free."
A teenage girls' choir from the United States, wearing mini-skirts and red waistcoats, mingled in the crowd while a man dressed as Santa Claus called out "Merry Christmas."

Away from Lima, villagers throughout this Andean nation held all-night vigils and marched through the streets where houses proudly displayed the red and white national flag as well as more traditional Christmas decorations.

The siege area around the residence has also become a macabre tourist attraction. On Wednesday, two flight attendants in Lima for the night, arrived to take photographs and share a drink with people outside the building before going to their airport hotel.

However, any flashes of traditional Christmas cheer were dimmed by ashen-faced policemen who watched over revellers and stopped them from setting off fireworks for fear of alarming the rebels inside the residence.
"We are just here carrying out instructions and ready to follow whatever orders we are given," said policeman Walter Toribio, who had been on duty there for a week.
He had sent his wife and two daughters away from Lima to the provinces, because he feared further guerrilla attacks in the capital if the siege was ended by force.
"Lima is a dangerous place to be right now. As much as I want to be with my family, I have sent them away because I want them to be safe," he said.
Since the 20 heavily-armed Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels stormed the Japanese ambassador's residence on Tuesday last week, they have freed 360 captives.
But they have remained firm on their principal demand that jailed comrades be released -- a demand President Alberto Fujimori flatly refuses to consider.
The hostages, including government officials, Japanese VIPs and some diplomats, were "in for a long haul" inside the cramped residence, according to Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto.

Cecilia Calle said her friend, Peru's state security chief Gen. Guillermo Bobbio, was considered an enemy by the MRTA guerrillas and would be one of the last hostages to be freed should a non-violent solution be reached.
"I know I will be here for many nights. I can only hope he is let out alive. That is what I'm praying for," said Calle, who was keeping vigil outside the residence.
